headline: Count the substrings in which one particular occurrence is unique
statement: For every nonempty substring of s, count letters occurring exactly once in that substring. Return the sum of these counts over all substring occurrences, including equal text at different indices.
constraints: s consists of uppercase English letters
The answer fits a signed 32-bit integer
intuition: Count the substrings in which one particular occurrence is unique. Its start must lie after the previous equal letter, and its end must lie before the next equal letter.
approach: Remember the previous two indices of each character, initially -1 and -1.
When a new occurrence i arrives, the former last occurrence p gets its right boundary i.
Add (p-before)*(i-p), then shift the remembered indices.
At the end, use len(s) as the next-occurrence boundary for each final occurrence.
correctness: For an occurrence at p with equal neighbors before and after, uniqueness requires start in before+1..p and end in p..after-1. Those independent choices give (p-before)*(after-p) substrings. Each unique letter of each substring corresponds to exactly one such occurrence, so summing contributions counts precisely the requested total.
bruteForce: Enumerate every substring and count its characters anew: O(n³) time; extending a frequency map improves this to O(n²).

complexity.explanation: Time O(n); auxiliary space O(σ), σ <= 26. Output storage is excluded unless stated.

pitfalls: Unique means exactly once, not merely distinct.
Use -1 and n as missing-neighbor boundaries.
Equal substring text at different positions still contributes separately.
